title: Depression after childbirth: support and treatment that can help
intro: Having a baby can bring joy alongside exhaustion, anxiety or sadness. Postnatal depression is more than a difficult day or a failure to be a good parent. It can begin during pregnancy or after birth and is treatable. You can ask for help even if you do not have every symptom, and you do not need to manage it alone.

sections.heading: Distinguish passing mood changes from a persistent problem
paragraphs: The baby blues usually begin soon after birth and settle within about two weeks. Persistent low mood, loss of enjoyment, guilt, hopelessness, marked anxiety or difficulty functioning need assessment, especially if symptoms worsen or last longer. Trouble sleeping even when there is an opportunity to rest, appetite changes and difficulty bonding can also occur. Do not wait for a particular duration if symptoms are severe. Depression can also affect fathers and partners, who may need support in their own right. Hormonal changes, previous illness, sleep disruption and social difficulties can interact; there is no single cause and no justification for blame.

sections.heading: Tell someone and arrange a full assessment
paragraphs: A family doctor, midwife, maternity team or mental health professional can help arrange care. Explain mood, sleep, fears, daily functioning and any thoughts about harm. A questionnaire may help identify symptoms, but a conversation and assessment are needed. Mention previous depression, bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis, family psychiatric history, medicines, birth complications and feeding arrangements. Physical conditions can contribute, including thyroid problems or anaemia, and may need investigation. Tell the team if language, transport, money, an unsafe relationship or fear of judgement makes seeking care difficult. Ask for practical help to overcome those barriers.

sections.heading: Urgent symptoms require a different response
paragraphs: Thoughts of self-harm or harming the baby should be discussed promptly with a clinician; unwanted frightening thoughts are not automatically the same as intending to act, but deserve support and assessment. If there is an intention or immediate risk, inability to keep yourself or the baby safe, or harm has occurred, seek emergency help now. Sudden confusion, hallucinations, unusual fixed beliefs, extreme overactivity or very little need for sleep may indicate postpartum psychosis, a medical emergency needing immediate assessment. Do not leave a severely unwell parent alone with responsibility for the baby while arranging help. Ask a trusted adult to stay and support safety, following emergency advice.

sections.heading: Treatment can include therapy, medicines and specialist care
paragraphs: Psychological treatments such as cognitive behavioural or interpersonal therapy can help. Antidepressants may be appropriate, sometimes alongside therapy, according to severity, previous response and preference. Discuss breastfeeding or pregnancy, the baby's health, possible side effects and monitoring with the prescriber; some medicines can be used during breastfeeding. Do not stop essential psychiatric treatment abruptly or assume you must stop breastfeeding to receive any care. Severe depression or psychosis may need urgent specialist or hospital treatment. Ask how appointments can fit around childcare and what to do if symptoms worsen before the next review. Progress may take time and the plan can be adjusted.

sections.heading: Make support specific and protect recovery
paragraphs: Practical help may include meals, shopping, sharing chores and arranging safe opportunities to rest. A trusted person can help book or attend an appointment with permission. Offer companionship without demanding instant happiness, bonding or gratitude. Agree manageable activities and realistic expectations rather than another list of parenting tasks. Feeding support should consider both infant nutrition and the parent's wellbeing. Keep follow-up even after improvement and discuss any medicine changes with the treating team. Before a future pregnancy, a previous perinatal episode is a reason to plan prevention and early support. Recovery varies; persistent symptoms deserve continued care, not shame.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: making help concrete
examples.text: Elena feels hopeless and cannot sleep even when her partner cares for the baby. Instead of only telling her to rest, the partner helps arrange a same-week clinical conversation, takes over shopping and agrees a practical rest plan. If safety concerns arise, they seek urgent help earlier.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: recognising an emergency
examples.text: Soon after birth, a parent becomes confused, barely sleeps and believes the baby has unusual powers. A relative recognises a sudden change, stays with the family and obtains emergency assessment instead of treating it as ordinary baby blues or waiting for a routine appointment.

questions: Could this be depression, anxiety or another condition that needs urgent treatment?
Which treatment fits my feeding situation, previous illness and preferences?
Who can help with daily care, and what is our plan if safety or symptoms worsen?
